**Martha Howe-Douglas** (born 1981 or 1982) is an English actress and writer. She is known as a member of the Them There collective with which she wrote and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_, _Yonderland_, and _Ghosts_. She also played receptionist Donna Parmar in the BBC One daytime soap _Doctors_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-1)
Howe-Douglas was born and raised in Moseley, a suburb of south Birmingham, England, in 1981 or 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-2) She attended Edgbaston High School.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-3) She graduated from RADA in 2003.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-ashbee.net-5)

After graduating from RADA, Howe-Douglas appeared in the Christmas special of _The Office_, as a receptionist at Wernham-Hogg.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-6) From 24 April 2006 until 11 May 2007, Howe-Douglas played receptionist Donna Parmar in the BBC daytime soap opera _Doctors_. For her role as Donna, Howe-Douglas received nominations for Best Comedy Performance and Best Newcomer at the 2007 British Soap Awards.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-2007_BSAs-7)
In 2009, she landed one of the main multi-role parts on a new children's TV history sketch show programme, CBBC's _Horrible Histories_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-8) where over five years and five series, she played numerous characters including the queens Cleopatra, Elizabeth I, Boudicea and Victoria. In 2011, she appeared in _The Proms_, in a special live "_Horrible Histories_ Big Prom Party" performance.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-9) In 2013, she co-created, co-wrote and co-starred in Sky1's series _Yonderland_, in which she played lead character Debbie Maddox[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-10) in all three series.

Howe-Douglas' other acting roles have included appearing in _The Armstrong & Miller Show_ on BBC One and playing Flora Dies-Early in the radio comedy show _Bleak Expectations_, as well as Lady Anne Woodstock in the radio show _The Castle_. In 2018, she appeared in the BBC soap opera _EastEnders_ as Annie Pritchard.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-11) From 15 April 2019, Howe-Douglas co-wrote, produced and starred in the BBC sitcom _Ghosts_, which sees her reunited with the _Horrible Histories_ cast.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-12)
Howe-Douglas is married to a photographer who worked on _Ghosts_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-13)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Martha Howe-Douglas |

**Martha Howe-Douglas** (born 1981 or 1982) is an English actress and writer. She is known as a member of the Them There collective with which she wrote and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_, _Yonderland_, and _Ghosts_. She also played receptionist Donna Parmar in the BBC One daytime soap _Doctors_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-1)
Howe-Douglas was born and raised in Moseley, a suburb of south Birmingham, England, in 1981 or 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-2) She attended Edgbaston High School.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-3) She graduated from RADA in 2003.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-ashbee.net-5)
texts.1:
After graduating from RADA, Howe-Douglas appeared in the Christmas special of _The Office_, as a receptionist at Wernham-Hogg.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-6) From 24 April 2006 until 11 May 2007, Howe-Douglas played receptionist Donna Parmar in the BBC daytime soap opera _Doctors_. For her role as Donna, Howe-Douglas received nominations for Best Comedy Performance and Best Newcomer at the 2007 British Soap Awards.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-2007_BSAs-7)
In 2009, she landed one of the main multi-role parts on a new children's TV history sketch show programme, CBBC's _Horrible Histories_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-8) where over five years and five series, she played numerous characters including the queens Cleopatra, Elizabeth I, Boudicea and Victoria. In 2011, she appeared in _The Proms_, in a special live "_Horrible Histories_ Big Prom Party" performance.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-9) In 2013, she co-created, co-wrote and co-starred in Sky1's series _Yonderland_, in which she played lead character Debbie Maddox[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-10) in all three series.
texts.2:
Howe-Douglas' other acting roles have included appearing in _The Armstrong & Miller Show_ on BBC One and playing Flora Dies-Early in the radio comedy show _Bleak Expectations_, as well as Lady Anne Woodstock in the radio show _The Castle_. In 2018, she appeared in the BBC soap opera _EastEnders_ as Annie Pritchard.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-11) From 15 April 2019, Howe-Douglas co-wrote, produced and starred in the BBC sitcom _Ghosts_, which sees her reunited with the _Horrible Histories_ cast.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-12)
Howe-Douglas is married to a photographer who worked on _Ghosts_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Howe-Douglas#cite_note-13)

**Ben Willbond** is an English actor and screenwriter best known as a member of the British Them There collective, for which he has written and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_, _Yonderland_, and _Ghosts_.
Along with fellow Them There member Laurence Rickard, he co-wrote the 2015 feature film _Bill_ and 2022 feature-length television comedy _We Are Not Alone_.
Willbond was a Forces child and consequently his family moved around every two years. He was sent to board at Stamford School in Lincolnshire, when he was nine years old. He was bullied whilst attending the school.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-2) Willbond, when talking about his experience at the school, said "I don't actually remember that time because it was so shocking".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-3) He studied Russian and French at [St Catherine's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Catherine's_College,_Oxford "St Catherine's College, Oxford").

Along with Arnold Widdowson, Willbond was part of the comedy duo "Ben & Arn", who won the Perrier Award for "Best Newcomer" in 1999,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) and formed the self-proclaimed "thinking man's French pop duo"[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-5) Priorité à Gauche.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Guardian20050817-6) He then went on to perform his solo character shows at several Edinburgh Fringe Festivals, the last being in 2005 which also starred Katy Brand and Jim Field Smith.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Guardian20050817-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-7)
He is perhaps best known for his regular role in CBBC's _Horrible Histories_, in which he played a wide variety of historical figures, most memorably recurring roles as Henry VIII and Alexander the Great. Along with the five other members of the _Horrible Histories_ starring cast, Willbond is also the co-creator, -writer and -star of _Yonderland_, a family fantasy comedy series that premiered on Sky One on 10 November 2013.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-8) In addition he is the co-writer of _Bill_, a BBC-produced comedy film based loosely around the early life of William Shakespeare, which involved the same starring troupe.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-9)

Previously, Willbond had starred in a short-lived sketch show for ITV2 called _Laura, Ben & Him_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) with Marek Larwood and sometime writing partner Laura Solon. He also appeared in Solon's BBC Radio 4 sketch show, _Laura Solon: Talking and Not Talking_. Other notable television work includes the recurring roles of Steve Warwick in the BBC comedy _Rev_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-BBCRevS2E4-10) Adam Kenyon in BBC Four's _The Thick of It_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) and as a television director in the movie-length final episode of the Ricky Gervais comedy _Extras_ (BBC Two).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) He has also appeared in _[Katy Brand's Big Ass Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy\_Brand's\_Big\_Ass\_Show "Katy Brand's Big Ass Show")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) for ITV2 and _Mayo_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-AvalonCV-11) for BBC One.
Willbond's other radio credits include BBC Radio 4 series _Deep Trouble_, _Double Science_ (co-written with Justin Edwards), _Recorded for Training Purposes_ and the first series of _Electric Ink_. He also starred in the YouTube romantic comedy_Nigel and Victoria_.
Willbond in 2011

His 2010 short film _[Tooty's Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooty's\_Wedding "Tooty's Wedding")_, which he co-wrote with Solon, won numerous international comedy awards and was screened as part of the 2012 Sundance Film Festival.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Huffington_20111215-12) Other notable film work includes the movie _Starter for 10_ (2006).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-13) In 2007 he had a short appearance in _[St Trinian's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St\_Trinian's\_(film) "St Trinian's (film)")_,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-AvalonCV-11) as a nervous school inspector.
Between 2019 and 2023, Willbond portrayed The Captain in the BBC sitcom _Ghosts_ with the other main _Horrible Histories_ cast.
Willbond has two children and is married to Charlotte Gordon. He is a keen cricketer and plays for the Thunderers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-14)

**Ben Willbond** is an English actor and screenwriter best known as a member of the British Them There collective, for which he has written and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_, _Yonderland_, and _Ghosts_.
Along with fellow Them There member Laurence Rickard, he co-wrote the 2015 feature film _Bill_ and 2022 feature-length television comedy _We Are Not Alone_.
Willbond was a Forces child and consequently his family moved around every two years. He was sent to board at Stamford School in Lincolnshire, when he was nine years old. He was bullied whilst attending the school.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-2) Willbond, when talking about his experience at the school, said "I don't actually remember that time because it was so shocking".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-3) He studied Russian and French at [St Catherine's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Catherine's_College,_Oxford "St Catherine's College, Oxford").
texts.1:
Along with Arnold Widdowson, Willbond was part of the comedy duo "Ben & Arn", who won the Perrier Award for "Best Newcomer" in 1999,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) and formed the self-proclaimed "thinking man's French pop duo"[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-5) Priorité à Gauche.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Guardian20050817-6) He then went on to perform his solo character shows at several Edinburgh Fringe Festivals, the last being in 2005 which also starred Katy Brand and Jim Field Smith.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Guardian20050817-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-7)
He is perhaps best known for his regular role in CBBC's _Horrible Histories_, in which he played a wide variety of historical figures, most memorably recurring roles as Henry VIII and Alexander the Great. Along with the five other members of the _Horrible Histories_ starring cast, Willbond is also the co-creator, -writer and -star of _Yonderland_, a family fantasy comedy series that premiered on Sky One on 10 November 2013.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-8) In addition he is the co-writer of _Bill_, a BBC-produced comedy film based loosely around the early life of William Shakespeare, which involved the same starring troupe.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-9)
texts.2:
Previously, Willbond had starred in a short-lived sketch show for ITV2 called _Laura, Ben & Him_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) with Marek Larwood and sometime writing partner Laura Solon. He also appeared in Solon's BBC Radio 4 sketch show, _Laura Solon: Talking and Not Talking_. Other notable television work includes the recurring roles of Steve Warwick in the BBC comedy _Rev_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-BBCRevS2E4-10) Adam Kenyon in BBC Four's _The Thick of It_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) and as a television director in the movie-length final episode of the Ricky Gervais comedy _Extras_ (BBC Two).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) He has also appeared in _[Katy Brand's Big Ass Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy\_Brand's\_Big\_Ass\_Show "Katy Brand's Big Ass Show")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-feca2011-4) for ITV2 and _Mayo_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-AvalonCV-11) for BBC One.
Willbond's other radio credits include BBC Radio 4 series _Deep Trouble_, _Double Science_ (co-written with Justin Edwards), _Recorded for Training Purposes_ and the first series of _Electric Ink_. He also starred in the YouTube romantic comedy_Nigel and Victoria_.
Willbond in 2011
texts.3:
His 2010 short film _[Tooty's Wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooty's\_Wedding "Tooty's Wedding")_, which he co-wrote with Solon, won numerous international comedy awards and was screened as part of the 2012 Sundance Film Festival.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-Huffington_20111215-12) Other notable film work includes the movie _Starter for 10_ (2006).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-13) In 2007 he had a short appearance in _[St Trinian's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St\_Trinian's\_(film) "St Trinian's (film)")_,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-AvalonCV-11) as a nervous school inspector.
Between 2019 and 2023, Willbond portrayed The Captain in the BBC sitcom _Ghosts_ with the other main _Horrible Histories_ cast.
Willbond has two children and is married to Charlotte Gordon. He is a keen cricketer and plays for the Thunderers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Willbond#cite_note-14)

**James Howick** (born 14 May 1979) is an English actor and writer, known for his appearances in television series such as _Peep Show_ (2007–2012), _Sex Education_ (2019–2022), and _Here We Go_ (2022–present). Howick is additionally associated with the creative collective Them There, with whom he has written and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_ (2009–2013), _Yonderland_ (2013–2016), _Ghosts_ (2019–2023), and _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_ (2026).
James Howick was born in Chichester, West Sussex on 14 May 1979, but grew up in Bognor Regis.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3) He was educated at The Regis School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-4) He graduated with First Class Honours from Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts in 2000.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-5)

Along with the five other members of the _Horrible Histories_ starring cast, which includes Ben Willbond, Martha Howe-Douglas, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby and Laurence Rickard, Howick is also the co-creator, -writer and -star of _Yonderland_, an eight-part family fantasy comedy series that premiered on Sky One on 10 November 2013.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-6) He co-starred with the same troupe in _Bill_, a BBC-produced comedy film based loosely around the early life of William Shakespeare.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-7) Other prominent television roles include Gerard in _Peep Show_, Gerry in Danny Boyle's _Babylon_ and Anthony in the revival of _Reggie Perrin_. In addition he has been a regular guest star in various sketch comedies, including _The Armstrong and Miller Show_ and _The Kevin Bishop Show_. In 2017, he played Aaron Mayford in the ITVthriller_Broadchurch_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-8) From 2019 to 2023, Howick featured in the Netflix original series _Sex Education_ as Mr Hendricks, a science teacher at Moordale Secondary School who also conducts the Swing Band. Howick is the co-creator, co-writer and co-star of the BBC One sitcom _Ghosts_, - Howick plays numerous characters, but is mostly known for his role as Patrick Butcher, a 1980s Scout Master who was killed in an archery accident - the show was first broadcast in 2019 and ran for five series. More recently, Howick was cast in the 2022 BBC comedy series _Here We Go_ in which he plays Paul Jessop.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-9)

In film, Howick played Cpl. Matlin in the 2004 Guillermo del Toro adaptation of _Hellboy_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)
Howick met his wife, Lauren, on the set of _Reggie Perrin_. They married in 2012 and live in East Finchley, London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)
Howick is an avid _Star Wars_ fan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-10)

**James Howick** (born 14 May 1979) is an English actor and writer, known for his appearances in television series such as _Peep Show_ (2007–2012), _Sex Education_ (2019–2022), and _Here We Go_ (2022–present). Howick is additionally associated with the creative collective Them There, with whom he has written and starred in productions including _Horrible Histories_ (2009–2013), _Yonderland_ (2013–2016), _Ghosts_ (2019–2023), and _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_ (2026).
James Howick was born in Chichester, West Sussex on 14 May 1979, but grew up in Bognor Regis.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3) He was educated at The Regis School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-4) He graduated with First Class Honours from Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts in 2000.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-5)
texts.1: Along with the five other members of the _Horrible Histories_ starring cast, which includes Ben Willbond, Martha Howe-Douglas, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby and Laurence Rickard, Howick is also the co-creator, -writer and -star of _Yonderland_, an eight-part family fantasy comedy series that premiered on Sky One on 10 November 2013.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-6) He co-starred with the same troupe in _Bill_, a BBC-produced comedy film based loosely around the early life of William Shakespeare.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-7) Other prominent television roles include Gerard in _Peep Show_, Gerry in Danny Boyle's _Babylon_ and Anthony in the revival of _Reggie Perrin_. In addition he has been a regular guest star in various sketch comedies, including _The Armstrong and Miller Show_ and _The Kevin Bishop Show_. In 2017, he played Aaron Mayford in the ITVthriller_Broadchurch_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-8) From 2019 to 2023, Howick featured in the Netflix original series _Sex Education_ as Mr Hendricks, a science teacher at Moordale Secondary School who also conducts the Swing Band. Howick is the co-creator, co-writer and co-star of the BBC One sitcom _Ghosts_, - Howick plays numerous characters, but is mostly known for his role as Patrick Butcher, a 1980s Scout Master who was killed in an archery accident - the show was first broadcast in 2019 and ran for five series. More recently, Howick was cast in the 2022 BBC comedy series _Here We Go_ in which he plays Paul Jessop.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-9)
texts.2:
In film, Howick played Cpl. Matlin in the 2004 Guillermo del Toro adaptation of _Hellboy_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)
Howick met his wife, Lauren, on the set of _Reggie Perrin_. They married in 2012 and live in East Finchley, London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-Guardian-3)
Howick is an avid _Star Wars_ fan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Howick#cite_note-10)

Laurence Carl Rickard (born 14 June 1975 in Brighton,
England
,
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland) is a film and television actor and screenwriter. As a member of the writing team for Horrible Histories, he won the BAFTA Children's Award for Best Writer at the 63rd British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA) Awards. His representative works include the series Yonderland, All Over the Place, and seasons two through five of Ghosts.
4
Since 2020, he has portrayed Robin and Humphrey's Head in seasons two through five of Ghosts, also contributing as a writer and creator on the series. The Ghosts: 2023 Christmas Special in which he appeared aired on the BBC in December 2023. The film Bad News, for which he served as a screenwriter, was released in December 2024, and the television series *My Amanda*
, on which he worked as a writer, premiered in February 2025. He has held dual roles as both actor and writer in numerous projects and maintains long-term collaborations with filmmakers such as Martha Howe-Douglas and
Ben Willbond
. The film
Ghosts: The Haunting of Barton Manor
, which he wrote and produced, was released in the UK on 23 October 2026.

His representative work(s) include Yonderland, the All Over the Place series, and seasons two through five of Ghosts. Since 2020, he has portrayed the characters Robin and Humphrey's Head in seasons two through five of Ghosts, and has also participated in writing and creating the series.

# An interview with Laurence Rickard (and an audience Q&A)
## this event features
### Laurence Rickard
Brighton-born Laurence Rickard is a BAFTA-winning writer and actor, best known for the TV comedies _Ghosts_ and _Horrible Histories_, along with a collective called Them There, also responsible for the fantasy sitcom _Yonderland_, of which Laurence was its showrunner. The autumn of 2026 saw the release of the acclaimed feature film _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_, based on the series, which ran from 2019 to 2023. _Ghosts_ was a huge success, earning three BAFTA nominations, in which he played the caveman, Robin, and the beheaded Sir Humphrey Bone, as well as co-writing it. He contributed to nearly sixty episodes of the series of _Horrible Histories_, the multi-award-winning historical and musical sketch comedy.
Laurence wrote the comedy film _Bill_, with Ben Willbond, a fictitious tale on the younger life of William Shakespeare. He has also written for shows such as _Amandaland_, _Tracey Ullman’s Show_, _Tracey Breaks the News_, also appearing in those two, _The Armstrong and Miller Show_, as well as the children’s animation _Peter Rabbit_.

# An interview with Laurence Rickard (and an audience Q&A)
## this event features
### Laurence Rickard
Brighton-born Laurence Rickard is a BAFTA-winning writer and actor, best known for the TV comedies _Ghosts_ and _Horrible Histories_, along with a collective called Them There, also responsible for the fantasy sitcom _Yonderland_, of which Laurence was its showrunner. The autumn of 2026 saw the release of the acclaimed feature film _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_, based on the series, which ran from 2019 to 2023. _Ghosts_ was a huge success, earning three BAFTA nominations, in which he played the caveman, Robin, and the beheaded Sir Humphrey Bone, as well as co-writing it. He contributed to nearly sixty episodes of the series of _Horrible Histories_, the multi-award-winning historical and musical sketch comedy.
Laurence wrote the comedy film _Bill_, with Ben Willbond, a fictitious tale on the younger life of William Shakespeare. He has also written for shows such as _Amandaland_, _Tracey Ullman’s Show_, _Tracey Breaks the News_, also appearing in those two, _The Armstrong and Miller Show_, as well as the children’s animation _Peter Rabbit_.

Title: Movie Review: Timothee’ goes “Wonka”
Chunks: 0,1,2
Hand it to Warner Bros. for their approach to their favorite piece of Roald Dahlintellectual property.
They didn’t just remake “Charlie” or “Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory.” They took a stab at giving us a back story about how “magician, inventor and chocolatier” Willy got his start.
They spared almost no expense in acquiring a big name cast, new music (by Neil Hannon and Jody Talbot), choreographing big new production numbers with more sprawling production design, giving us something like the most spectacular**“Wonka”**ever.
They cannily hired the wit behind “Paddington” to direct and co-write it and make the chocolate trains run on time.
With **Hugh Grant, Keegan Michael Key, Rowan Atkinson**, Oscar winners**Olivia Colman**and **Sally Hawkins**on board, the only worry might have been **Timothée Chalamet** in the title role. And he gives the chocolatier a light, upbeat touch. There’s none of writer-Roald’s sinister, punishing edge in Young Willy.
And Chalamet can sing, showing off a lilting, pleasant movie musical (not Broadway ready) voice, holding his own in some pretty impressive dance numbers, and selling his chocolate with an off-center twist.
“Hover chocolates?” They not only let you fly, they’re “salted with the bittersweet tears of a Russian clown.”
“Wonka” is a musical comedy that bowls you over with bigness — big stars, big sets, big numbers and big whimsy in service of a story that takes Willy from a ship’s cook gig on a fanciful fantasy film freighter to an unnamed 1930s EuroCity where he does battle with the singing, dancing, back-stabbing “chocolate cartel” (**Paterson Joseph, Mathew Banyton** and **Matt Lucas**).
“The greedy beat the needy” is their motto, and the movie’s cautionary message.
Willy’s got his tiny chocolate factory in a traveling trunk, unusually delicious and large beans that he stole from Oompa Loompa land — which a lone Loompa (Grant) is hellbent on stealing back, in bean or Wonka Chocolate form.

All he has to do is escape an enslaving laundry run by villains played by Colman and**Tom Davis,** where young Noodle (**Calah Lane**) and Abacus Crunch (“Downton’s” own **Jim Carter**) are among those working off their debt. He’s got to dodge the chocolate-craving/ever-fattening-up chief of police (Key) and his minions and outfox the cartel.
All if he wants to manifest the “destiny” his late mother (Hawkins) urged him into.
The new music’s good, if forgettable, which is why “The Oompa Loompa” song and that “Pure Imagination” theme song from the ’60s songsmiths Leslie Bricusse and Anthony Newley are reprised and sampled here.
No, it doesn’t have much of Roald Dahl’s trademark darkness. But Dahl daftness? Sure.
I was never a huge fan of the Gene Wilder film that made “Willy” a pop culture touchstone. “Wonka,” for what its worth, drags and sags through its middle acts before freshening up for a big, long finale.
But all involved have managed to back-engineer a prequel into that “classic” original, and not embarass anybody in the process — save for Hugh Grant as “the little orange man” with green hair. And he’s in on the joke.
It’s light and fun and when all else fails, which it seldom does, the sheer scale of it all, that “bigness,” bowls you over and lets you and the kids leave the cinema with a big grin, and a big craving for chocolate before you get home.
Rating:PG (Some Violence|Mild Language|Thematic Elements)
Cast: Timothee Chalamet, Hugh Grant, Calah Lane, Keegan Michael Key, Paterson Joseph, Simon Farnaby, Matt Lucas, Sally Hawkins, Rowan Atkinson, Jim Carter and Olivia Colman.
Credits: Directed by Paul King, scripted by Simon Farnaby and Paul King. A Warner Bros. release.
Running time: 1:58

Title: How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material

## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Bringing this to screen and expanding the parents’ presence was part of “getting a bigger story that would fit an hour and a half or thereabout,” the writer explains. “Without wanting to criticize Enid Blyton, [the books are] fairly simple. They go up [a ladder], someone loses something, or they have to get something before they go down. It’s quite quick — all in a few pages.”
There was also “dealing with the old-fashionedness and bringing it up-to-date,” Farnaby continues. “The big thing in the books was that the kids really want to go to the countryside. They go, ‘Great! There’ll be wood, and I can play in the trees and eat cakes all day long.’ I don’t know any kid that speaks like that now.”
“I wanted to just have brilliant kids. They’re not likable to start. They are abrasive and we had feedback that ‘it’s too much.’ But then they transform,” adds Gregor. “The further the starting point, the bigger the transformation. When Beth says ‘Ok, I’ll join the family project,’ it’s a very down-low moment. I had to keep going to her [Gadsdon], to give less so that when she did give, it [was] meaningful.”
Farnaby’s work on projects like _Paddington 2_, _Wonka_ and _Ghosts_ well captures these kinds of dichotomies. _In The Magic Faraway Tree_, it’s a balance between funny and heartfelt that Gregor brings to life within a visual framework he calls the Blytopia. “What that means is imaginative, a sort of Heath Robinson-ish ingenious because there’s a lot of ingenuity in the lands. Claire Foy’s Polly is ingenious the way she uses salvaged stuff and her design skills to make random stuff,” he tells _THR_. “But keep it humble and modest. There was no plastic on set. I didn’t film one item of plastic in the whole film as a shorthand for everyone. Everything looked rougher — made of wood or old metal. It was a bit more found.”
_The Magic Faraway Tree_ Palisades Park Pictures

## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Bringing the grander “spectacle but modesty, humility but epicness” of Blyton’s magic tree, its lands and residents to the screen required both practical sets and a VFX department created just for the film. “There was no whole tree, because I wanted it to breathe. So we made our own visual effects company. We had a load of old servers, computers and electric fans and way too many of them plugged into the extension cables. It looked like some kind of dark web crypto farm above St James’s Park Tube Station in an abandoned headquarters of the subway,” he tells _THR_. “What it meant was the VFX are as handcrafted as all of the physical things.”
And while the director says he loves the VFX and the team of respected artists that became “like a little family,” he “built as many sets as I could” in an effort to balance Blyton’s fantastical and natural universe. Amid an assemblage of various sections equating to a three-story-high tree, sets featured fully constructed locations like Moonface’s house and Dame Washalot’s deck, alongside cushions rigged to lift the actors into the air. Filming was a highly physical experience, with the movie’s young actors having to traverse the tree with the help of climbing lessons and abseiling gear.
“The kids had to be amazed for real. So under the tree with the flowers, when you go in there through the veil, I wanted it to be like going into a rhododendron den,” says Gregor. “The Land of Goodies was edible, and yes, there’s huge giant sweets everywhere, but they’re growing on the trees. It’s a natural place.”
This “blytopia” philosophy extended to the characters themselves. “What I did with Moonface, it got some heat when the trailer came out because people were like, ‘You changed him too much. He should be Moonface, not Moon-Hair.’ But I just had a number of things that I wanted to do as part of my Blytopia,” the director explains. “Nonso is a fantastic actor, and to put him in a big white mask or VFX and cover his face, I just thought, why? I want to see his face. I want to see him connect.”

## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
The choice was also partly inspired by Gregor’s experience on the BBC series _Black Ops_, which allowed him to “witness the power of Black hair and how amazingly expressive it all is. So I thought, what about a big crescent afro?” he tells _THR_. “[Nonso’s] face is darker, and there’s a dark side of the moon. His coat is dark on one side and light on the other. It’s all about the phases of the moon.”
In the script, Farnaby leaned into Blyton’s datedness as “kids find those old-fashioned traits quite funny. I liked that and definitely wanted to use the quaintness,” he tells _THR_. “For me, it was keeping the vibe of Enid Blyton in the tree and all those fun characters, but having it come colliding with the modern world. The tree people hadn’t had any modern kids for a while because Moonface said, ‘Let’s not have humans anymore,’ so they were all a bit old-fashioned.”
With a character like Silky, “she likes tea and cakes, and hasn’t heard of feminism, so that Beth can teach her something.” Farnaby understood The Saucepan Man as “a bit of a bad joke — that he can’t hear very well — you wouldn’t necessarily come up with now.” But his daughter found him funny the film, “it’s not that he’s deaf. He wears saucepans as an eccentric life choice, even though it means he can’t hear people, which I love.”
The children also provided the opportunity to shift away from certain depictions in Blyton’s writing. It’s why Beth, and not her brother Joe, is the oldest sibling in the film. “There’s a bit of casual sexism in her books — ‘You’re nearly as good as a boy’ — so the boy in [the film], he’s lovable, but he’s not ‘Come along, everyone. Keep up, girls.’ It just felt too 1950s.”
Moonface (Nonso Anozie) and Dame Washalot (Jessica Gunning).Palisades Park Pictures

## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Since the film’s release overseas, some Blyton fans have appreciated the changes more than others. “On IMDb we don’t have a huge rating and I asked, ‘Why is that?’ I looked at it the other day, and it’s people who go, ‘Why isn’t it exactly like the books? Like exactly? Like why don’t they just film the books?’” Farnaby tells _THR_. “No disrespect to those people, but that is not going to be a good movie because you’ll have 20 very short stories with no connection, and it will all be sort of same-y.”
“I have a lot of respect for how loved a book is,” says Gregor. “It’s never the same as in your head, so I don’t expect to be as good as what’s in people’s minds. But I think everybody can see how full-hearted we were. And if you do something with love, even if it is different, people can acknowledge that’s not how it was in my head, but it was fine.”
Ahead of the film’s U.S. theatrical release, Farnaby is unsure whether Blyton’s work will garner the same reactions among Americans. They may have less familiarity with the beloved books than the U.K., where the film has become the top-grossing indie film in the first half of 2026, and is the latest in a line of book adaptations, alongside _Project Hail Mary, Wuthering Heights_ and _Hamnet,_ to bolster the regional box office. But after successful theatrical runs in places like Britain, Australia and Poland for Vertical, he is sure the movie’s Friday opening could cement future sequels. According to Gregor, there’s already a foundation of an idea for at least one immediate sequel. “When you grow up, you lose the idea of magic and that’s a central tenet of film — and certainly the main thing we want to explore in this sequel, which we will hopefully get to do,” he tells _THR_.

## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Bringing this to screen and expanding the parents’ presence was part of “getting a bigger story that would fit an hour and a half or thereabout,” the writer explains. “Without wanting to criticize Enid Blyton, [the books are] fairly simple. They go up [a ladder], someone loses something, or they have to get something before they go down. It’s quite quick — all in a few pages.”
There was also “dealing with the old-fashionedness and bringing it up-to-date,” Farnaby continues. “The big thing in the books was that the kids really want to go to the countryside. They go, ‘Great! There’ll be wood, and I can play in the trees and eat cakes all day long.’ I don’t know any kid that speaks like that now.”
“I wanted to just have brilliant kids. They’re not likable to start. They are abrasive and we had feedback that ‘it’s too much.’ But then they transform,” adds Gregor. “The further the starting point, the bigger the transformation. When Beth says ‘Ok, I’ll join the family project,’ it’s a very down-low moment. I had to keep going to her [Gadsdon], to give less so that when she did give, it [was] meaningful.”
Farnaby’s work on projects like _Paddington 2_, _Wonka_ and _Ghosts_ well captures these kinds of dichotomies. _In The Magic Faraway Tree_, it’s a balance between funny and heartfelt that Gregor brings to life within a visual framework he calls the Blytopia. “What that means is imaginative, a sort of Heath Robinson-ish ingenious because there’s a lot of ingenuity in the lands. Claire Foy’s Polly is ingenious the way she uses salvaged stuff and her design skills to make random stuff,” he tells _THR_. “But keep it humble and modest. There was no plastic on set. I didn’t film one item of plastic in the whole film as a shorthand for everyone. Everything looked rougher — made of wood or old metal. It was a bit more found.”
_The Magic Faraway Tree_ Palisades Park Pictures
texts.5:
## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Bringing the grander “spectacle but modesty, humility but epicness” of Blyton’s magic tree, its lands and residents to the screen required both practical sets and a VFX department created just for the film. “There was no whole tree, because I wanted it to breathe. So we made our own visual effects company. We had a load of old servers, computers and electric fans and way too many of them plugged into the extension cables. It looked like some kind of dark web crypto farm above St James’s Park Tube Station in an abandoned headquarters of the subway,” he tells _THR_. “What it meant was the VFX are as handcrafted as all of the physical things.”
And while the director says he loves the VFX and the team of respected artists that became “like a little family,” he “built as many sets as I could” in an effort to balance Blyton’s fantastical and natural universe. Amid an assemblage of various sections equating to a three-story-high tree, sets featured fully constructed locations like Moonface’s house and Dame Washalot’s deck, alongside cushions rigged to lift the actors into the air. Filming was a highly physical experience, with the movie’s young actors having to traverse the tree with the help of climbing lessons and abseiling gear.
“The kids had to be amazed for real. So under the tree with the flowers, when you go in there through the veil, I wanted it to be like going into a rhododendron den,” says Gregor. “The Land of Goodies was edible, and yes, there’s huge giant sweets everywhere, but they’re growing on the trees. It’s a natural place.”
This “blytopia” philosophy extended to the characters themselves. “What I did with Moonface, it got some heat when the trailer came out because people were like, ‘You changed him too much. He should be Moonface, not Moon-Hair.’ But I just had a number of things that I wanted to do as part of my Blytopia,” the director explains. “Nonso is a fantastic actor, and to put him in a big white mask or VFX and cover his face, I just thought, why? I want to see his face. I want to see him connect.”
texts.6:
## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
The choice was also partly inspired by Gregor’s experience on the BBC series _Black Ops_, which allowed him to “witness the power of Black hair and how amazingly expressive it all is. So I thought, what about a big crescent afro?” he tells _THR_. “[Nonso’s] face is darker, and there’s a dark side of the moon. His coat is dark on one side and light on the other. It’s all about the phases of the moon.”
In the script, Farnaby leaned into Blyton’s datedness as “kids find those old-fashioned traits quite funny. I liked that and definitely wanted to use the quaintness,” he tells _THR_. “For me, it was keeping the vibe of Enid Blyton in the tree and all those fun characters, but having it come colliding with the modern world. The tree people hadn’t had any modern kids for a while because Moonface said, ‘Let’s not have humans anymore,’ so they were all a bit old-fashioned.”
With a character like Silky, “she likes tea and cakes, and hasn’t heard of feminism, so that Beth can teach her something.” Farnaby understood The Saucepan Man as “a bit of a bad joke — that he can’t hear very well — you wouldn’t necessarily come up with now.” But his daughter found him funny the film, “it’s not that he’s deaf. He wears saucepans as an eccentric life choice, even though it means he can’t hear people, which I love.”
The children also provided the opportunity to shift away from certain depictions in Blyton’s writing. It’s why Beth, and not her brother Joe, is the oldest sibling in the film. “There’s a bit of casual sexism in her books — ‘You’re nearly as good as a boy’ — so the boy in [the film], he’s lovable, but he’s not ‘Come along, everyone. Keep up, girls.’ It just felt too 1950s.”
Moonface (Nonso Anozie) and Dame Washalot (Jessica Gunning).Palisades Park Pictures
texts.7:
## How ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Embraced Its Dated Source Material
Since the film’s release overseas, some Blyton fans have appreciated the changes more than others. “On IMDb we don’t have a huge rating and I asked, ‘Why is that?’ I looked at it the other day, and it’s people who go, ‘Why isn’t it exactly like the books? Like exactly? Like why don’t they just film the books?’” Farnaby tells _THR_. “No disrespect to those people, but that is not going to be a good movie because you’ll have 20 very short stories with no connection, and it will all be sort of same-y.”
“I have a lot of respect for how loved a book is,” says Gregor. “It’s never the same as in your head, so I don’t expect to be as good as what’s in people’s minds. But I think everybody can see how full-hearted we were. And if you do something with love, even if it is different, people can acknowledge that’s not how it was in my head, but it was fine.”
Ahead of the film’s U.S. theatrical release, Farnaby is unsure whether Blyton’s work will garner the same reactions among Americans. They may have less familiarity with the beloved books than the U.K., where the film has become the top-grossing indie film in the first half of 2026, and is the latest in a line of book adaptations, alongside _Project Hail Mary, Wuthering Heights_ and _Hamnet,_ to bolster the regional box office. But after successful theatrical runs in places like Britain, Australia and Poland for Vertical, he is sure the movie’s Friday opening could cement future sequels. According to Gregor, there’s already a foundation of an idea for at least one immediate sequel. “When you grow up, you lose the idea of magic and that’s a central tenet of film — and certainly the main thing we want to explore in this sequel, which we will hopefully get to do,” he tells _THR_.

# Ghosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-off
Picking up not long after the events of the final episode of the BBC’s haunted house comedy, this glorious new film is every bit as warm and comforting as the TV sitcom
Cath Clarke
Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.00 BST Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.06 BST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google
W hat on earth is happening at Button House? Kitty has tasered a police officer. Fanny is pulling down her capacious Victorian drawers to show off her bottom. Robin the caveman has fallen in love with a crusty eco activist (to be fair she looks quite a bit like him). If you’ve never watched the BBC’s haunted house comedy Ghosts – one of the finest family television shows in recent memory – none of the above will make the slightest bit of sense. Neither perhaps will this glorious new film, which picks up with the ghosts not long after the events of the final episode in 2023.
Often when British sitcoms get a spin-off what happens is the gag-to-runtime ratio dips. But breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness. The jokes keep coming, and it’s every bit as warm and comforting as on TV.
Video 3

# Ghosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-off
It’s been a few months since Alison and Mike (Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe) left Button House, selling the crumbling stately pile to a hotel chain. But work on the refurb has stalled, and the ghosts are pining after Alison, the only living person who can see them (long story). One of the joys of Ghosts is the competing main character energy of Button House’s deceased residents, played to perfection by an unassailable cast. There’s the sleazy Tory MP with no trousers, Julian Fawcett (Simon Farnaby), forever caught with his pants down. And scoutmaster Pat (Jim Howick) with an arrow through his neck. It feels mean to leave out the rest; each and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script. To say anything about the plot would ruin the fun. (I watched with a nine-year-old who hooted throughout.) It really is a delight.
Ghosts: The Possession of Button House is in UK and Irish cinemas from 23 October

B utton House is a haunted estate set on acres of land steeped in history. It’s home to a coterie of ghosts whose deaths have intersected with the estate in various ways. Bound by the grounds’ perimeter, these spirits include Kitty Higham (Lolly Adefope), a childlike aristocrat; Thomas Thorne (Mathew Baynton), a tortured Romantic poet; Julian Fawcett (Simon Farnaby), a corrupt MP who died with his trousers down, so to speak; Lady Fanny Button (Martha Howe-Douglas), a wronged gentlewoman — yes, yes, ‘Fanny Button’, like a clitoris; grow up — Pat Butcher (Jim Howick), an unfortunate Scout leader who died on the archery range; Robin (Laurence Rickard), a caveman from before modern housing was even a thing; and the Captain (Ben Willbond), whose rugged masculinity, he likes to think, conceals the love that dared not speak its name.

_Ghosts_ fans will know the best part of any series was the on-set bloopers that were released after the end of every series. Thankfully, it looks like the cast gave plenty of material for a bloopers video after the release of new movie, _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_.
To mark the upcoming release of the highly-anticipated movie, **Digital Spy** has an **exclusive** behind-the-scenes featurette that sees the cast reflect on reuniting for the new movie, as well as footage of the cast cracking up on set.
Namely, Jim Howick making Mathew Baynton laugh over a line about chicken, leading to Howick making himself laugh. Enjoy the set footage above right now.
Lionsgate
**Related: BBC's _Ghosts_ movie reveals game-changing twist in hilarious new trailer**
In the featurette, Martha Howe-Douglas said it was "really special" to come back for the _Ghosts_ movie, while Howick noted that it wasn't that hard to get back into their characters: "We were able to tap into them quite quickly."
"Within ten minutes, you're just all laughing," added Laurence Rickard.

# Exclusive: Ghosts cast crack up in hilarious new filming footage for upcoming movie
## What to Read Next
It seems as though the creators also made _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_ work for series newcomers as well. Although if you haven't watched all five series of _Ghosts_ already, we're not sure what else you've been doing.

"There are Easter eggs in there for the series fans. Also we've made something for an audience that hasn't seen the series before," Howick explained.
Simon Farnaby summed it up quite nicely though: "Being together, it's sort of like coming home."
No, _you're_ crying.
Lionsgate
**Related: "Unmissable" _Ghosts_ movie confirms its runtime**
The featurette also appears to confirm that _Fleabag_ and _Ludwig_ star Sian Clifford is in the movie as she's seen towards the end on set with Rickard.
We don't have any extra information on who she's playing, whether that's a ghost or not, but it looks like she was having a great time on set as we all would be.
Ahead of its release in cinemas this month, it's been confirmed that _Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_ has a runtime of 97 minutes and has been classified a PG for "mild scary scenes, rude humour, violence, language, drug references".
**_Ghosts: The Possession of Button House_ is released in UK cinemas on 23 October.**

# Ghosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-off
Picking up not long after the events of the final episode of the BBC’s haunted house comedy, this glorious new film is every bit as warm and comforting as the TV sitcom
Cath Clarke
Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.00 BST Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.06 BST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google
W hat on earth is happening at Button House? Kitty has tasered a police officer. Fanny is pulling down her capacious Victorian drawers to show off her bottom. Robin the caveman has fallen in love with a crusty eco activist (to be fair she looks quite a bit like him). If you’ve never watched the BBC’s haunted house comedy Ghosts – one of the finest family television shows in recent memory – none of the above will make the slightest bit of sense. Neither perhaps will this glorious new film, which picks up with the ghosts not long after the events of the final episode in 2023.
Often when British sitcoms get a spin-off what happens is the gag-to-runtime ratio dips. But breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness. The jokes keep coming, and it’s every bit as warm and comforting as on TV.

# Ghosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-off
It’s been a few months since Alison and Mike (Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe) left Button House, selling the crumbling stately pile to a hotel chain. But work on the refurb has stalled, and the ghosts are pining after Alison, the only living person who can see them (long story). One of the joys of Ghosts is the competing main character energy of Button House’s deceased residents, played to perfection by an unassailable cast. There’s the sleazy Tory MP with no trousers, Julian Fawcett (Simon Farnaby), forever caught with his pants down. And scoutmaster Pat (Jim Howick) with an arrow through his neck. It feels mean to leave out the rest; each and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script. To say anything about the plot would ruin the fun. (I watched with a nine-year-old who hooted throughout.) It really is a delight.
Ghosts: The Possession of Button House is in UK and Irish cinemas from 23 October
